messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Years ago, during a period of political unrest that tore through the Latin American neighborhood where he grew up, Mateo was detained by captors wearing strict, unmarked uniforms. They spoke to him in a rapid, incomprehensible dialect that signaled immediate threat, and when he expected protection, the authorities simply locked the gates and walked away. For weeks, he endured systematic torture, leaving him with absolutely no answers about his captors and the quiet certainty that those who wielded power over him would face no consequences. This event fundamentally rewired his threat appraisal system, transforming a specific historical violation into a permanent state of hyperarousal. Now, a headline about political violence or the sudden murmur of a crowd speaking an incomprehensible dialect instantly pulls him back into the full sensory reliving of the past. When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once, with partial clarity where some moments of event are extremely clear while others are completely blank. These unavoidable cues do not merely startle him; they reinforce his conviction that the people or institutions that should have protected him let me down, and that accountability is an illusion. His deep-seated belief that the world remains hostile and that he has lost my connection to my community and culture actively primes his nervous system, allowing the traumatic memories to surface with renewed visceral intensity. Because he has come to view institutions as perpetually corrupt, he grows hyper-vigilant to the very environmental cues that first signaled danger, treating a passing authority figure as a present-tense threat. The overwhelming weight of the reliving dictates his daily survival as a practicing psychiatrist. To escape the onslaught, he stops going out to neighborhood gatherings, and when he must see patients in his own clinic, he spends hours rehearsing what to say before any interaction. He actively redirects his mind to clinical protocols the moment fear rises, convincing himself he is merely being professionally thorough. Paradoxically, this redirection and avoidance temporarily suppress the intrusion, but because the trauma remains cognitively unprocessed, the memories eventually return with sharper, unbidden force. Each time the unprocessed event floods his awareness, it deepens his certainty that he has truly lost his connection to his culture and that those who wielded power over him will face no justice. His retreat from social spaces confirms to him that institutional failure is a permanent reality, solidifying his isolation and cementing the conviction that he is permanently disconnected from his community. By systematically avoiding public spaces, he has shrunk his world so drastically that when he inevitably encounters a uniformed hospital security guard in his building lobby or hears related news on the television in his waiting room, the absence of a broader safety routine makes those triggers feel overwhelmingly immediate. At sixty-two, the sheer exhaustion of maintaining this rigid architecture of fear is what finally brought Mateo to seek help. He no longer wishes to erase the past, only to reclaim the ability to sit in his own office without bracing for an ambush, hoping to find a way to trust his own senses again without the constant specter of institutional betrayal looming over him. His decades of training in psychopharmacology now feel like hollow shields against the visceral weight of the past, and the silence of his single apartment echoes the same institutional void he experienced decades ago. He came to therapy not to relive the torture, but to finally dismantle the daily habits that have kept him locked in its shadow.
